drills.q: A function passes mypy --strict cleanly but throws a TypeError at runtime on data from an external API. What went wrong, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Type hints are erased at runtime -- mypy only guarantees internal consistency under the assumption that declared types match actual values, which it can't verify for external data. Fix: add explicit runtime validation (a Pydantic model, isinstance checks) at the trust boundary where external data enters.

drills.q: mypy rejects a call passing an actual list[Dog] variable to a parameter typed list[Animal], even though the function body never mutates the list. What's the fix and why does it work?
drills.a: Change the parameter type to Sequence[Animal] (covariant, read-only) instead of list[Animal] (invariant). Since Sequence excludes mutation, list[Dog] safely satisfies Sequence[Animal] -- the fix correctly reflects that the function only reads, never writes, through this parameter.

drills.q: A code reviewer questions why list[T] must be invariant while Iterator[T] can be covariant. Give the concrete unsafe scenario that justifies the difference.
drills.a: If list[Dog] were covariant with list[Animal], code holding the Animal-typed alias could legally .append(Cat()) into what is, underneath, an actual list[Dog], silently inserting a wrong subtype. Iterator[T] only ever produces values (no input/write position), so Iterator[Dog] safely substitutes for Iterator[Animal] with no way to smuggle a wrong type in.

drills.q: Your team just bumped a Pydantic v1 dependency pin to v2 expecting it to be a drop-in upgrade. What breaks, and what's the actual migration effort?
drills.a: Real API surface changed: @validator -> @field_validator/@model_validator, class Config -> model_config=ConfigDict(...), .dict()/.json() -> .model_dump()/.model_dump_json(). v2 also has stricter default coercion than v1 in several cases. bump-pydantic automates the mechanical renames, but custom validators and config usage need manual review since automated tooling can't safely infer intent behind v1-specific coercion reliance.

drills.q: You're designing a library function that should accept 'anything file-like' (has .read() and .close()), used by callers you don't control. Protocol or ABC, and why?
drills.a: Protocol -- callers can pass any object with the right shape (a real file, BytesIO, a test double, a third-party file-like object) without needing to retrofit inheritance from your library's base class, which matters since some callers are outside your control. This mirrors how Python's actual duck typing already permits calling .read()/.close() regardless of class hierarchy.

drills.q: You later need to add a shared default implementation (e.g. a mixin providing .close() that calls .read() for cleanup) to the file-like interface from the previous question. Does Protocol still work?
drills.a: No -- Protocol only describes a shape, providing no mechanism for shared implementation code to be inherited. Genuine shared behavior requires an actual base class (possibly an ABC) that callers explicitly inherit from. Conflating 'I want type compatibility' with 'I want shared implementation' is the mistake to avoid here.

drills.q: Explain why Callable[[Arg],Ret] is contravariant in Arg but covariant in Ret simultaneously, and why this isn't a contradiction.
drills.a: For parameters (input position), accepting a broader type is safe (a function handling any Animal can substitute for one handling only Dog) -- contravariant. For return values (output position), producing a narrower type is safe (a function returning only Dog can substitute for one expected to return any Animal) -- covariant. These are different positions within the same generic type, each independently governed by the substitution-safety argument for that position, which is a correctly-modeled case of mixed variance, not a contradiction.

drills.q: Why is Pydantic v2's Rust core meaningfully faster on large nested JSON specifically, and does that mean validation is now effectively free?
drills.a: v2 compiles annotations once into composable Rust validators executed largely outside Python's per-field interpreter overhead, which v1 paid per field -- this overhead compounds most on large, deeply-nested payloads, which is exactly where the 5-50x speedup is largest. It is not free: validation cost still scales with data size/complexity, just at a much lower constant factor than v1.
